proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀pá-Ìwọ̀n kì í parọ́ fún Aláṣọ; òtítọ́ la fi ń díwọ̀n ayé. (The measuring rod never tells a lie to the cloth merchant; it is with absolute truth that the universe is measured: Teaching rigorous honesty and objective standards in civic commerce.)
Bí ọ̀pá kò bá tọ́, aṣọ kò lè tò lẹ́sẹẹsẹ. (If the measuring rod is crooked, the cut cloth can never drape in balance: Demonstrating that flawed standards produce disordered institutions.)

Ẹni tí ó mú ọ̀pá-ìwọ̀n lọ́wọ́ kì í rẹ́ ará rẹ̀ jẹ. (He who holds the standard measuring rod in his own hand never cheats his neighbor: Affirming that self-regulation and personal integrity prevent communal exploitation.)
Ọ̀pá-Ìwọ̀n.provenance_and_citations: Eicher, Joanne B. (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles; Ojo, G.J. Afolabi (1966). Yoruba Culture: A Geographical Analysis; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Bí ìmọ́lẹ̀ ìràwọ̀ bá pọ̀ tó bẹ́ẹ̀ gẹ́gẹ́, kì í fọ́ ojú òru. (Even when the light of the stars multiplies across the sky, it never blinds the night, it merely illuminates the path: Emphasizing gentle guidance and illuminating leadership that guides without overwhelming.)

Ìràwọ̀ kì í sọnu lójú ojúmọ́; orí l’a fi ń mọ ọ̀nà. (The stars never truly vanish from the heavens at dawn; it is with inner consciousness that the traveler charts his course: Teaching that ancestral truths remain steadfast even when unseen.)
Ẹní ń wo ìràwọ̀ kì í kọsẹ̀ lábẹ́ òkùnkùn. (He who navigates by the ancient stars never stumbles into the pitfalls of darkness: Affirming that cosmological wisdom guards against earthly ruin.)
Ìra-Ìràwọ̀.provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Ojo, G.J. Afolabi (1966). Yoruba Culture: A Geographical Analysis; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àbò-irin kì í bẹ̀rù ọfà; àyà gbígbó la fi ń wolẹ̀ ogun. (The forged breastplate of iron harbors no fear of the piercing arrow; it is with brave heart that one marches onto the battlefield: Teaching fortitude and protective resilience against malice.)
Irin Ògún kò ṣeé bẹ́rẹ̀ sí í jẹ láì ní àṣẹ. (The consecrated iron of Ògún cannot be worn without solemn sanction: Reminding warriors that military might must submit to moral covenant.)
Ẹni tí ó wọ àbò-irin kì í sá fún ìṣẹ́lẹ̀. (He who is clad in the iron armor of truth never flees from sudden turmoil: Exhorting leaders to maintain structural composure under crisis.)
Abo-Irin.provenance_and_citations: Ajayi, J.F.A. & Smith, Robert S. (1964). Yoruba Warfare in the Nineteenth Century; Smith, Robert S. (1988). Kingdoms of the Yoruba; Falola, Toyin (1984). The Political Economy of a Pre-colonial African State: Ibadan, 1830–1900.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọṣẹ kì í bá omi jà kí ó má kùfọ́; ìwà mímọ́ ló ń fa àlàáfíà wá. (Soap never mingles with clear water without generating luxuriant foam; spiritual purity always attracts divine peace: Teaching that righteous deeds naturally bear auspicious fruit.)

Ewé ọṣẹ ló ń fọ ẹ̀tẹ́ dànù; ẹni tó mọ̀ ọ́n lò kì í rí àbùkù. (It is the sacred soap leaf that washes away dishonor; he who applies ancestral wisdom never suffers public disgrace: Affirming the restorative power of moral purification.)

Omi tútù la fi ń gbó ewé ọṣẹ; ìfọ̀kanbalẹ̀ ni baba ìwòsàn. (With cool spring water is the soap leaf prepared; inner tranquility is the ultimate sovereign healing: Enforcing the principle of coolness and patience.)
Ewe-Ose.provenance_and_citations: Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Bascom, William (1951). Yoruba Food.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹni tí ó jẹ àgbàbò ọba, yóò bá ọba wọ̀gbẹ́; àṣẹ kì í ṣe ti ẹnìkan. (He who relishes the supreme honors of the king must accompany the sovereign into the sacred grove of transition: Teaching that elite privilege carries profound, irrevocable communal accountability.)

Ọba kì í kú lásán; àwọn awo ló ń sin ọlá lọ sí ọ̀run. (A crowned king never departs this mortal coil alone; it is the initiates of state mysteries who escort sovereign majesty into the ancestral realm: Illustrating royal transition protocols.)

Oyè ń bọ̀ lẹ́yìn ikú; orúkọ rere ní ń dúró títí láé. (Title and mortal splendor dissolve in death, but virtuous character and a noble name endure across eternity: Affirming the absolute primacy of Ìwà-rere.)
Abobaku.provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Lloyd, P.C. (1962). Yoruba Land Law; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gẹlẹdẹ Spectacle.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọjà l’ayé, ọ̀run n’ilé; Òsì Ìyalájé kì í jẹ́ kí ètò ọjà rú. (The world is a bustling marketplace; the otherworld is our eternal home; the deputy queen of commerce never allows the marketplace to collapse into disorder: Enforcing judicial equity and ethical trading.)

Bí Ìyalájé kò bá sí, Òsì rẹ̀ ní ń dá owó ọjà lẹ́jọ́. (In the absence of the commerce sovereign, her left-hand lieutenant arbitrates market fiscal disputes: Signifying seamless institutional governance and continuity.)

Ọ̀tún ń gbé ọjà, Òsì ń tọ́jú owó; àpapọ̀ wọn ni àṣẹ. (The right-hand regulates the trades, the left-hand safeguards the treasury; together they uphold sovereign economic harmony: Demonstrating collective administrative equilibrium.)
Osi-Iyalaje.provenance_and_citations: Awe, Bolanle (1992). Nigerian Women in Historical Perspective; Oyěwùmí, Oyèrónkẹ́ (1997). The Invention of Women: Making an African Sense of Western Gender Discourses; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: A kì í fi àró tẹ́ aṣọ kí ó má dídán; àtijọ́ la ti ń dáró ọlá. (One does not immerse woven fabric into ancestral indigo without it emerging radiant; it is from deep antiquity that we dye the robes of majesty: Celebrating the transformative dignity of guild labor.)

Ojú odò-àró kì í bẹ̀rù aró; ẹni tí ó forí tì í ló ń d'ọlọ́lá. (The mouth of the dye pit never dreads the pungent indigo; he who perseveres through rigorous discipline becomes crowned with honor: Teaching artisanal tenacity.)
Àró kì í pa aṣọ lára; ẹwà ló ń fún un. (The deep indigo dye never destroys the cloth; it bestows protective luster and cultural dignity: Illustrating that discipline ennobles character.)
Odo-Aro.provenance_and_citations: Eicher, Joanne B. (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles; Ojo, G.J. Afolabi (1966). Yoruba Culture: A Geographical Analysis; Lamb, Venice & Holmes, Judy (1980). Nigerian Weaving.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹja àbò kì í kọ̀ omi tútù; àlàáfíà ló ń bá ẹni tó wọ̀ ọ́ gbé. (The sacred mudfish never rejects cool living waters; spiritual serenity and prosperity abide with the wearer: Calling down fertility and harmonious fortune.)

Àbò l’orí aṣọ, aró l’orí ọlá; a kì í wọ àdìrẹ k'ojú ó tì wá. (The mudfish motif crowns the textile, deep indigo crowns majesty; one never wears sacred Adire and encounters public disgrace: Symbolizing lineage pride.)

Omi jinlẹ̀ l'ẹja ń lúwẹ̀ẹ́; àṣẹ ń bẹ l’ọ́wọ́ aláṣọ. (In deep waters the mudfish swims with grace; sovereign authority rests within the hand of the master dyer: Linking artistic craft with spiritual command.)
Adire-Abo.provenance_and_citations: Eicher, Joanne B. (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles; Abiodun, Rowland (2014). Yoruba Art and Language: Seeking the African in African Art; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹni tí ó gbé epo kọjá ọjà kì í bẹ́rẹ̀ sí í ju òkúta. (He who carries a calabash of red palm oil across the crowded marketplace does not engage in stone-throwing: Teaching that vulnerability and sacred value demand caution, diplomatic patience, and emotional restraint.)

Bí Ògún bá ń bínú, ẹpo pupa la fi ń rọ̀ ọ́. (When Ògún blazes with martial fury, it is red palm oil that softens his wrath: Illustrating the metaphysical power of gentle, cooling offerings to pacify destructive wrath.)

Ẹpo nìtẹ́lẹ̀ ẹ̀jẹ̀; kò sí ẹni tí kì í jẹ ẹ́po. (Palm oil is the terrestrial surrogate of blood; there is no living soul who does not partake of its life-giving sustenance: Affirming universal dependence on ancestral nutrition and peaceful communion.)

Epo ni mọ̀ ọn jẹ, n kò mọ̀ ọn jẹ̀jẹ̀. (It is red palm oil that I consume, I have no commerce with mortal blood: Spoken by righteous initiates to proclaim moral innocence, dedication to peace, and unblemished character.)
Ẹpo-Pupa.provenance_and_citations: Bascom, William (1951). Yoruba Food; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Verger, Pierre (1995). Dieux d'Afrique / Òrìṣà: Les Dieux Yorouba en Afrique et au Nouveau Monde; Eicher, Joanne B. (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òrí kì í fojú d'oòrùn kó má yọ́; sùúrù ló ń ṣẹ́gun ìwà líle. (The shea butter never confronts the midday sun without dissolving; gentle patience inevitably triumphs over rigid stubbornness: Emphasizing the power of soft persistence and moral yielding.)

Òrí tútù la fi ń tù Ọ̀rìṣà lójú; ooru kì í kọ́lé àlàáfíà. (With cool, fragrant shea butter do we pacify the countenance of the divinities; volatile anger never builds a sanctuary of peace: Teaching emotional restraint.)

Ẹni tí ó fi òrí para kì í kọ ojú sí iná. (He who has anointed his body with smooth shea butter does not draw near the open flames: Warning against reckless provocation when one carries precious blessings.)
Ori-Amo.provenance_and_citations: Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Ojo, G.J. Afolabi (1966). Yoruba Culture: A Geographical Analysis.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹni tí ó wọ bàtà ilẹ̀kẹ̀ kì í tẹ ẹrẹ̀ nù; ọlá kì í fọwọ́ rọ́ ẹ̀tẹ́. (He who wears beaded royal shoes does not step into muddy corruption; sovereign honor never compromises with indignity: Teaching moral vigilance for those endowed with leadership.)

Ilẹ̀kẹ̀ kì í dákẹ́ láì fọwọ́ kọ ọlá; owó la fi ń ra ìyùn. (Sacred beads never remain unnoticed without proclaiming prestige; it is with noble wealth that royal coral is acquired: Highlighting the spiritual and economic weight of regalia.)

Àtòpọ̀ ilẹ̀kẹ̀ ní ń jẹ́ kí adé Ọba dán. (It is the patient aggregation of individual beads that makes the monarch's crown gleam: Emphasizing that supreme authority is built on collective communal unity.)
Ilekere.provenance_and_citations: Drewal, H.J. & Mason, John (1998). Beads, Body, and Soul: Art and Light in the Yoruba Universe; Abiodun, Rowland (2014). Yoruba Art and Language: Seeking the African in African Art; Willett, Frank (1967). Ife in the History of West African Sculpture.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òkúta kì í kú, bẹ́ẹ̀ ni kì í rùn; òtítọ́ inú ń dúró títí láé. (The carved stone neither perishes nor rots; inner truth and ancestral covenants endure across all generations: Affirming the permanence of sacred history against mortal decay.)

Àwọn ère Ẹ̀sìẹ́ kò fẹnu sọ̀rọ̀, ṣùgbọ́n wọ́n ń kọ́ ọmọ ayé lẹ́kọ̀ọ́. (The stone images of Ẹ̀sìẹ́ speak with no vocal tongue, yet they instruct all humanity in solemn reverence: Teaching that silent historical monuments hold sovereign civilizational authority.)
Ẹni tí ó mọ ìpìlẹ̀ ẹ̀re kì í fi ọwọ́ lásán kàn án. (He who understands the divine origins of the stone sculptures never approaches them with profane disrespect: Enforcing spiritual boundaries.)
Esi-Ike.provenance_and_citations: Stevens, Phillips (1978). The Stone Images of Esie, Nigeria; Willett, Frank (1967). Ife in the History of West African Sculpture; Shaw, Thurstan (1978). Nigeria: Its Archaeology and Early History.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògún ló ni irin, Ifẹ̀ ló ni àṣà; àpapọ̀ wọn ni a fi ń mọ ọlá. (Ògún owns the raw metallurgical power of iron, but Ilé-Ifẹ̀ owns the enduring aesthetic culture; from their sacred union is civilizational majesty molded: Celebrating royal metallurgy.)

Irin t'ó kọjá nínú iná kì í bẹ̀rù agbẹ̀dẹ. (The copper and iron that have passed through the blazing crucible fear neither the blacksmith's hammer nor the sculptor's chisel: Teaching endurance through trial.)

Ifẹ̀ kò l'ẹ́gbẹ́ nínú idẹ; ìmọ̀ àtijọ́ ló bí i. (Ilé-Ifẹ̀ has no equal in the casting of copper and brass; it was divine primordial knowledge that gave it birth: Affirming West African metallurgical primacy.)
Irin-Ife.provenance_and_citations: Willett, Frank (1967). Ife in the History of West African Sculpture; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art; Shaw, Thurstan (1978). Nigeria: Its Archaeology and Early History.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹṣin kì í fò kọjá ọ̀sá tí a kọ́ pẹ̀lú ọgbọ́n; àbò ilé ni àbò ẹ̀mí. (A cavalry steed cannot leap across a defensive trench engineered with ancient tactical wisdom; the fortification of the town is the preservation of human life: Teaching civil protection.)
Ọ̀sá ogun kì í gbẹ́ lásán; ẹ̀ṣọ́ la fi ń ṣọ́ odi. (A military trench is never excavated in vain; it is with disciplined guards that the perimeter wall is defended: Emphasizing tactical vigilance.)

Ẹni tí kò mọ ọ̀sá kò gbọ́dọ̀ gun ẹṣin ogun. (He who is blind to the defensive fortifications must never ride a charger into combat: Warning against reckless adventurism without tactical intelligence.)
Osa-Ogun.provenance_and_citations: Smith, Robert S. (1988). Kingdoms of the Yoruba; Ajayi, J.F.A. & Smith, Robert S. (1964). Yoruba Warfare in the Nineteenth Century; Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Iná kì í jó lórí òkè kí ó má fi èéfín hàn; àkíyèsí ni baba ẹ̀ṣọ́. (Fire never blazes on the mountain summit without revealing its smoke to the vigilant; sharp observation is the foundation of military defense: Teaching early warning and state readiness.)
Àmì iná ló ń ránṣẹ́ sí ìlú; ẹni tó rí i kì í sùn. (The beacon fire on the ridge sends urgent warning to the kingdom; he who beholds it does not slumber: Exhorting guardians to instant readiness.)

Orí òkè la ti ń gbóhùn ogun; ológun t'ó gbọ́n kì í dúró dè wàhálà. (From the mountain heights is the rumbling of war detected; a prudent general never waits for disaster to breach the palace gate: Promoting proactive defense.)
Aro-Ogun.provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Smith, Robert S. (1988). Kingdoms of the Yoruba; Falola, Toyin (1984). The Political Economy of a Pre-colonial African State: Ibadan, 1830–1900.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Bí Ìlù Ogun bá dún, ọ̀rọ̀ kò gbà áyè àṣeré; ológun a mú idà dání. (When the war drum resounds, idle play gives way to absolute purpose; the warrior grasps his blade with solemn resolve: Signifying the transition from civilian ease to disciplined duty.)

Ohùn ìlù ogun kò ṣeé fi etí lásán gbọ́; àṣẹ Ọba ló ń kọ́ ọ. (The tactical cadence of the military drum cannot be deciphered by untrained ears; it is the sovereign decree of the King that directs its rhythms: Teaching that force must obey legitimate authority.)
Ìlù tí a fi pè l'awo la fi ń lé ọ̀tá. (The very drum that gathers the martial guild is that which scatters the adversary into disarray: Illustrating acoustic coordination in warfare.)
Ilu-Ogun.provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Euba, Akin (1990). Yoruba Drumming: The Dùndún Tradition; Smith, Robert S. (1988). Kingdoms of the Yoruba.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: A kì í fi ẹ̀jẹ̀ Ògún pa Ògún lẹ́rù; àjọṣe àwọn Balógun ló ń bori ogun. (One does not intimidate Ògún with the sight of blood; it is the strategic consensus of the war council that conquers the adversary: Teaching that wisdom and unity surpass raw violence.)

Lábẹ́ igi àkòko la ti ń gbìmọ̀ ogun; ọ̀rọ̀ àìgbọ́ kì í wọ àfin. (Beneath the sacred Akòko tree do commanders deliberate their battle strategy; dissenting division must never breach the royal council: Enforcing military secrecy and solidarity.)

Ipade ogun kì í ṣe ti ẹ̀rù; ọkùnrin la fi ń wá àlàáfíà ilé. (The council of war is not convened for the faint of heart; it is through disciplined courage that enduring peace is secured for the homeland: Highlighting that defense serves peace.)
Ipade-Ogun.provenance_and_citations: Ajayi, J.F.A. & Smith, Robert S. (1964). Yoruba Warfare in the Nineteenth Century; Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Falola, Toyin (1984). The Political Economy of a Pre-colonial African State: Ibadan, 1830–1900.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Akéwì kì í ṣubú sọ́rọ̀; Ọ̀rúnmìlà ló ń fẹnu ránṣẹ́ sí i. (The royal bard never stumbles in his recitations; it is divine wisdom that guides his vocal tongue: Affirming that the imperial chronicler operates under ancestral inspiration and exact truth.)

Ewì tí ó ti ẹnu àgbà jáde kì í yẹ̀; oríkì ni àpótí ìtàn. (The poetic verse that issues from the mouth of the elder never fails; the royal chant is the indestructible ark of historical memory: Celebrating oral historiography.)

Bí Ọba kò bá gbọ́ ewì ìbàlà, ayẹyẹ kò tíì kún. (If the sovereign does not receive the solemn ancestral chant, the coronation rites remain incomplete: Affirming the constitutional necessity of oral praise poetry.)
Ewi-Ibala.provenance_and_citations: Barber, Karin (1991). I Could Speak Until Tomorrow: Oriki, Women and the Past in a Yoruba Town; Isola, Akinwumi (1998). Contemporary Yoruba Drama; Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àlọ́ o! Àlọ̀! — Ọgbọ́n la fi ń kọ́ ọmọ, a kì í fi òmùgọ̀ ṣètò ilé. (The riddle sounds, the chorus answers! — It is with analytical wit that the young are nurtured; one never builds a lineage on intellectual laziness: Enforcing communal education through dialogue.)

Àlọ́ kì í purọ́ lásán; àpèjúwe ìwà rere ló ń kọ́ni. (The folk riddle never weaves fables in vain; it instructs the listener in the nuanced anatomy of virtuous character: Teaching philosophical morality through metaphor.)
Ẹni tí ó yanjú àlọ́ àrògangan, òun ló jogún ọgbọ́n àwọn àgbà. (He who deciphers the complex philosophical riddle inherits the accumulated discernment of the ancestors: Celebrating mental acuity.)
Alo-Aragbe.provenance_and_citations: Abrahams, Roger D. (1983). African Folktales; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Babalola, Adeboye (1966). The Content and Form of Yoruba Ijala.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òsanyìn aṣọ̀rọ̀ bọ́rọ̀kọ̀; ewé gbogbo ló lògùn fún ẹni tí ó mọ̀ ọ́n lò. (Òsanyìn who speaks through the subterranean root; every single leaf is sovereign medicine for him who possesses the discernment to apply it: Reaffirming the sacred potency of nature.)

Ewé ìyọ́ kì í ta kókó sí egbò; àmúkúrò ìrora ló ń fún ará. (The healing salt-leaf never aggravates an open wound; it bestows swift soothing relief upon the suffering flesh: Teaching compassionate alleviation of pain.)

Omi ewé la fi ń bọ̀wọ̀ fún ẹ̀mí; àìlera kò ní bori awo. (With the living extract of sacred leaves do we pay homage to life; infirmity shall never vanquish the initiated healer: Affirming indigenous medical efficacy.)
Ewe-Ìyọ́.provenance_and_citations: Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìyá ni wúrà, baba ni dígí; Ìyá-Ìlé kì í jẹ́ kí ilé tuka. (Mother is pure gold, father is a protective mirror; the Senior Matriarch never permits the ancestral compound to fracture into discord: Emphasizing female governance and domestic solidarity.)

Bí Ìyá-Ìlé bá fọwọ́ sọ̀rọ̀, àlàáfíà ń jọba nínú agbo-ilé. (When the Matriarch of the compound speaks her counsel, peace and reconciliation reign throughout the family: Recognizing maternal judicial authority.)

Ẹni tí ó bọ̀wọ̀ fún Ìyá-Ìlé, yóò tẹ́wọ́ gba ìbùkún àwọn ìyá. (He who accords reverence to the senior compound matriarch shall receive the protective blessings of the ancestral mothers: Honoring maternal spiritual primacy.)
Ìyá-Ìlé.provenance_and_citations: Oyěwùmí, Oyèrónkẹ́ (1997). The Invention of Women: Making an African Sense of Western Gender Discourses; Awe, Bolanle (1992). Nigerian Women in Historical Perspective; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àrọ̀kìn kì í parọ́, bẹ́ẹ̀ ni kì í da ohun àtijọ́ rú; àkọsílẹ̀ ẹnu ní ń bọ́lá fún ilé. (The Royal Chronicler never fabricates lies, nor does he corrupt the ancient traditions; the oral archive preserves the unbroken majesty of the realm: Enforcing historical accuracy.)

Ọ̀rọ̀ ìṣẹ̀mbáyé kì í kú; ẹnu tí a fi ń sọ ọ́ ní ń sọ d'ọtun. (The archaic lore of primordial antiquity never dies; the generations that recount it keep it perpetually new: Teaching cultural endurance through recitation.)
Ẹni tí ó kọ̀ ọ̀rọ̀ àwọn àgbà á dákẹ́ sí àìròtẹ́lẹ̀. (He who rejects the ancestral historical chronicles shall stumble into unforeseen calamity: Cautioning against civilizational amnesia.)
Ọ̀rọ̀-Ìṣẹ̀̀mbátí.provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Biobaku, Saburi O. (1957). Sources of Yoruba History; Barber, Karin (1991). I Could Speak Until Tomorrow: Oriki, Women and the Past in a Yoruba Town.

proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀bẹ tí ó bẹ ẹran Ọba kì í jẹ́ kí ẹ̀jẹ̀ rẹ̀ sọnù lásán; àṣẹ ni a fi ń pín ọlá. (The consecrated blade that processes the King's banquet meat never allows blood to spill in vain; it is with sovereign order that royal bounty is apportioned: Teaching equity in royal distribution.)

Ọwọ́ agbẹ̀dẹ t'ó ṣe ọ̀bẹ ọba gbọ́dọ̀ mọ́ tónítóní. (The hand of the blacksmith who forged the royal ceremonial cleaver must be spiritually clean and pure: Enforcing guild sanctity in palace instruments.)

Ẹran ọba kì í ṣe ti àjẹkù; àwọn olóyè ló ń pín ọlá rẹ̀. (The royal sacrificial meat is never consumed carelessly; it is the titled chiefs who distribute its sacred portion: Preserving courtly etiquette.)
Ọ̀bẹ-Ẹran-Ọba.provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Rev. Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Abiodun, Rowland (2014). Yoruba Art and Language: Seeking the African in African Art.

Fìlà.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity (Ilé-Ifẹ̀, c. 11th–14th Century CE): Worn as woven coronets and soft caps by nobles and priest-chiefs depicted on archaeological terracotta heads. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ Period (14th–18th Century CE): Evolved into distinctive lineage and office insignia (notably Fìlà Gọ̀bí, Fìlà Abetí Ajá, and Fìlà Ọ̀ránmíyàn) tailored from handwoven Aṣọ-Òfì. Transatlantic Diaspora: Maintained by Lucumí and Candomblé practitioners as liturgical headgear (Gorra / Filá) honoring Orisha lineages. Modern Era: The universal crown of the Yorùbá man across international diplomacy, statecraft, and festive society.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Fìlà tó wọ̀ lórí kì í jẹ́ kí ẹ̀tẹ́ dé; orí t'ó gbọ́n ní ń gbé adé ọlá. (The noble cap seated upon the head prevents dishonor from descending; it is the head endowed with wisdom that upholds the crest of majesty: Teaching self-respect, dignity, and moral poise.)

A kì í wọ aṣọ ọlá kí a fi orí sílẹ̀ láìní fìlà. (One does not clothe oneself in robes of majesty while leaving the head unadorned by a cap: Demonstrating that character and civic etiquette require complete refinement.)

Bí fìlà bá tẹ́ lórí, a kì í bínú bọ́ ọ sọnù; títún un ṣe la fi ń gbọ́n. (When a cap sits askew upon the brow, one does not angrily fling it away; it is by readjusting it with patient care that one displays wisdom: Exhorting reform rather than destruction.)
Fìlà.provenance_and_citations: Eicher, Joanne B. (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles; Abiodun, Rowland (2014). Yoruba Art and Language: Seeking the African in African Art; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art.

Odù Ifá.historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Antiquity (c. 8th–12th Century CE): Systematized by Ọ̀rúnmìlà Bara Agbọnnirégún at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as the sovereign oral binary matrix of 256 chapters (16 Olódù Méjì + 240 Àmọ̀lù Odù) encoding total metaphysical science, medicine, ethics, and civilizational history. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ Period (14th–18th Century CE): Entrenched as the constitutional oracle of the Aláàfin, consulted by the imperial Oyomesi to inaugurate dynasties and ratify treaties. Transatlantic Middle Passage: Preserved through phenomenal oral retention by captured Babaláwos in Cuba (codified as Tratado Enciclopédico de Ifá) and Brazil (Merindilogún). Contemporary Era: Inscribed in 2005 by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ifá kì í purọ́, Ọ̀rúnmìlà kì í ṣèké; bí ayé ń yí padà, òtítọ́ inú odù kò ní yẹ̀. (Ifá never lies, nor does Ọ̀rúnmìlà practice deceit; though the earthly world shifts and wavers, the inner truth inscribed within the sacred Odù remains eternal and immutable: Teaching that moral truth and cosmic order are permanent foundations against mortal vicissitudes.)

Ẹni tó mọ Odù Ifá ló mọ ọ̀rọ̀ ayé; àkọsílẹ̀ àìkú ni àwọn awo ń kà nínú ìyẹ̀ròsùn. (He who understands the sacred chapters of Odù understands the deep mysteries of the universe; it is an imperishable metaphysical scripture that the initiates read upon the sacred divination dust: Affirming that the 256 Odù encapsulate total civilizational wisdom, ethical judgment, and cosmic science.)

Ojú Odù mẹ́rìndínlógún ni àpótí ìmọ̀; ẹni tí ó bá tẹ̀ ẹ́ kì í dáràn nílé ayé. (The sixteen primordial principal Odù constitute the sovereign treasury of wisdom; whoever anchors their life to their moral decrees shall never stumble into ruin in this terrestrial realm: Reaffirming that observance of spiritual taboos and ethical character secures divine protection.)
Odù Ifá.provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifa; Abimbola, Wande (1976). Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art.
